title: The borrowed telescope
text:
Bu Ratna, who had taught science at the village school for forty years, lent Dimas her telescope on a Sunday afternoon. It arrived wrapped in an old batik cloth, carried as carefully as if it were a sleeping baby.

“Saturn is low in the east this week,” she said, passing it over the fence. “Look for a bright star that does not twinkle. That will be the planet.”

Dimas thanked her three times and carried the telescope up to the balcony. He set it on its tripod, wiped the lens gently with a soft cloth and waited for darkness.

Darkness came. So did the clouds.

On Monday, a grey blanket covered the whole sky. On Tuesday, it rained so hard that the gutters overflowed and the frogs in the paddy field sang all night. On Wednesday, Dimas stood on the balcony until his mother had called him in for dinner three times.

“The sky does not care about your plans,” said his older sister, Wulan, without looking up from her book.

By Friday, Dimas had given up. He wrapped the telescope in its batik cloth and carried it next door. A borrowed thing, his grandfather always said, should go home in better shape than it left.

Bu Ratna was watering her orchids when he knocked. She looked at the bundle in his arms, then up at the sky above the rooftops.

“Not yet,” she said. “Clouds move. Patience is part of astronomy.”

So Dimas carried the telescope home again. At half past nine, a cool wind pushed the clouds westwards like a broom sweeping a floor. One steady point of light appeared above the mango tree.

His hands trembled as he turned the focus wheel. The blur sharpened, and there it was: a tiny golden ball wearing a thin, tilted ring.

For a moment, he forgot to breathe. Then he raced downstairs, past Wulan, out of the gate and next door, without even stopping for his sandals.

“Bu Ratna! It has a ring! It really has a ring!”

The old teacher smiled as if she had been waiting all week to hear those words.
